title: How Partnerships Fail From the Inside
summary: Most partnerships that collapse are not killed by the market. They are killed from inside, by one of three mechanisms: one partner capturing the decisions, one partner sitting on both sides of a deal, or terms that were never written down. This lesson names all three and the control that stops each.
body:
Partnerships rarely die from a bad market alone. They die from inside, through captured decisions, related-party dealing and handshake terms, and every one of those three can be seen and stopped early if you know where to look.

Recall

Q. When a broker introduces a landowner to you, what should be agreed before the first meeting?

A. Who the broker acts for, what fee is payable, when it is earned, and for how long after introduction it survives. Put it in writing. A fee dispute after closing is a fight you have already lost time on.

Q. Name the four broad stakeholder groups around a project.

A. The delivery team (contractors and consultants), the authorities that approve and inspect, the capital (lenders and investors), and the community around the site. Each has different power over your timeline.

Q. In a lender negotiation, what is usually easier to win, a lower rate or a looser covenant?

A. Often a looser covenant or a longer cure period, because it costs the lender little if the project performs. That is commercial practice, not a rule, and it varies by lender.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a developer is a professional partner. Almost every project you run will have at least one other party with money or land in it: an investor, a landowner, a co-developer, a lender with approval rights. The partnership is the operating system of the project. If it fails, a good site, a good design and a good lender cannot save it.

This is the second post-mortem week of the course. Week 46 looked at failures of debt and leverage. This week looks at failures of law, tax and partnership: the ones where the money was fine and the people were not. Cole, our auditor, sits beside me all week, because these failures leave a paper trail, and an auditor reads paper differently from an optimist.

Mechanism one: governance capture

In plain English: one partner ends up making the decisions that were meant to be shared, and the others find out late.

The professional term is governance capture. It means control over decisions, information or money concentrates in one party in a way the partnership documents did not intend. It almost never happens by a dramatic seizure. It happens by convenience. The managing partner holds the bank login because someone has to. The managing partner prepares the reports because the others are busy. The managing partner signs a small contract without a vote because the next meeting is three weeks away. Each step is reasonable. Together they hand one person the steering wheel, the speedometer and the map.

Applied example, hypothetical. Two partners each own half of a small apartment project. The agreement says any contract over 250,000 dollars needs both signatures. Over eighteen months the managing partner signs eleven contracts, each just under 250,000 dollars, for work that is really one package worth about 2,700,000 dollars. No single act breaks the agreement. The pattern defeats it. The control is to define major decisions by substance, not by a single number: aggregate related contracts, and require the other partner to see the full contract register every month, not just a summary.

Watch for three early signs of capture. Reports that summarise rather than show. Decisions announced as done rather than proposed. And a growing list of things the other partner "does not need to worry about". Each one is small. Each one is a step away from shared control.

Mechanism two: related-party dealing

In plain English: one partner is on both sides of a deal with the partnership.

A related-party transaction is any deal between the partnership and a person or company connected to one of the partners: the sponsor's own construction company, a property manager owned by a relative, a loan from an affiliate. These deals are not wrong in themselves. Many good developers run their own construction or management arm, and it can be cheaper and faster. The danger is that the connected partner sets the price and approves the price. No one negotiates against themselves.

Applied example, hypothetical. A sponsor's affiliated contractor is awarded a 20,000,000 dollar contract without competition. A market bid would have been about 19,000,000 dollars. The extra 1,000,000 dollars comes straight out of the project's profit, shared by everyone, and lands in the affiliate, owned by one person. On Day 3 we will put numbers on exactly how that shifts returns.

Say that out loud now.

The control has three parts: disclose the relationship in writing before the deal, benchmark the price against at least one independent quote or an independent cost consultant, and have the decision made by the partners who are not connected.

Mechanism three: the handshake deal

In plain English: the partners agreed on something important, and only one version of it exists, in two different memories.

A handshake deal is an agreement whose key terms were never written down. It feels like trust. In practice it is a dispute on a delay timer. Memories are not neutral. When land doubles in value after rezoning, the partner who contributed the land remembers "we would value it fairly later", and the partner who contributed cash remembers "the land went in at cost". Both may be honest. Both cannot be right. The timer goes off when the value moves.

The control is boring and absolute: write the economic terms down before money or land moves, even if it is a one-page term sheet signed by both. Contribution values, who decides what, how profit is split, what happens if one partner wants out. A lawyer turns it into a full agreement later. The one page stops the memories drifting.

Applied example, hypothetical. A landowner contributes a site worth 2,000,000 dollars at cost to a joint venture with a cash partner, on a handshake that the land "would be valued fairly". Two years later the site is rezoned and is now worth 3,500,000 dollars. The landowner wants the higher figure as his capital account. The cash partner wants the original figure. The difference decides who owns more of the profit, and on Day 5 we will see it is worth more than a million dollars either way. Nobody lied. Nobody wrote it down.

How the best do it

Large institutional joint ventures treat all three mechanisms as standing risks, not as insults to anyone's character. A common practice is a related-party policy attached to the joint venture agreement: every connected contract must be disclosed, priced against market by an independent consultant, approved by the non-conflicted side, and listed in every quarterly report. Another is a shared data room where both partners see the bank statements and the contract register directly, not through the manager's summary. A small developer can copy both on day one. Neither costs much. Both make you a partner that serious investors want to back again.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: related-party pricing above market can be challenged by a tax authority as well as by your partner; keep the benchmark. Liability: a partner who approves his own deal may face personal claims for breach of duty. Banking: lenders ask about affiliated contracts and expect them disclosed. Governance: define major decisions by substance and aggregate related contracts. Estate: a handshake term cannot be enforced by an executor who never heard it. Exit: a buyer's due diligence will find every undisclosed related-party deal, and price it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that all three mechanisms feel like efficiency, not danger, while they are happening. The control is a quarterly governance review in which the non-managing partner checks the decision log, the related-party list and the signed terms against what actually happened.

The beginner's mistake

Thinking that writing the terms down signals distrust. It signals professionalism. The partner who resists one page of written terms is telling you something.

Callback

In Week 69 we built partner agreements: vesting, deadlock, capital calls. Every clause in that week is a defence against one of today's three mechanisms. Deadlock clauses stop capture; approval rules stop related-party dealing; the written agreement itself ends the handshake.

Recap

Partnerships fail from inside through governance capture, related-party dealing and handshake deals. The controls are substantive major-decision rules, independent pricing and approval of connected deals, and written terms before value moves.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: Enron, and what happens when the finance chief sits on both sides of the deal.
checklist: I can name the three internal failure mechanisms of a partnership.
My agreements define major decisions by substance and aggregate related contracts.
Every related-party deal is disclosed in writing before it is approved.
Every related-party price is benchmarked against an independent quote.
Only non-conflicted partners vote on a related-party deal.
Economic terms are written and signed before land or money moves.
The non-managing partner sees the bank statements and contract register directly.
I hold a quarterly governance review against the decision log.
head: Field checklist
speak: Partnerships rarely die from the market. They die from inside, in three ways. First, governance capture: decisions that were meant to be shared slowly move into one partner's hands, through convenience, not conspiracy. The control is to define major decisions by substance, aggregate related contracts, and give every partner direct access to the bank statements and contract register. Second, related-party dealing: one partner sits on both sides of a deal, such as the sponsor's own construction company winning the build contract. That is not wrong in itself, but the connected partner cannot both set and approve the price. The control is written disclosure, an independent price benchmark and a vote by the partners who are not connected. Third, the handshake deal: key terms that exist only in memory, which drift apart the moment value moves. The control is one signed page of economic terms before land or money changes hands. All three feel like efficiency while they happen. That is exactly why you check.
terms: Governance capture — the drift of control over decisions, information or money into one party beyond what the partnership documents intended.
Related-party transaction — a deal between the partnership and a person or company connected to one of its partners.
Handshake deal — an agreement whose key terms were never written down, so each party holds its own version.

hostile.q: Your affiliated company is building this project. Why should I believe the contract price is fair?
hostile.a: Because you should not have to believe it. Here is the independent cost consultant's benchmark against two outside bids, the written disclosure of my interest, and the approval minute signed by the partners who have no connection to the contractor. The affiliate's contract is listed in every quarterly report, and any change order over the agreed limit comes to you for approval.

title: Enron: When the Finance Chief Sat on Both Sides
summary: Enron collapsed into bankruptcy in December 2001 after years of deals between the company and partnerships run by its own chief financial officer. This lesson takes the case through seven steps and draws one rule for any developer who will ever deal with a connected party.
body:
Enron did not fail because one trade went wrong. It failed because its board allowed its own finance chief to run outside partnerships that dealt with the company, and then trusted the reports that the same people prepared.

Recall

Q. What are the three internal ways a partnership fails?

A. Governance capture, related-party dealing and handshake deals. Each feels like efficiency while it is happening.

Q. In a deal pipeline, why track conversion rates by stage?

A. Because it tells you how many early leads you need to close one deal, and shows you which stage is leaking, so you fix the leak instead of just adding leads.

Q. Under a joint venture agreement, what is a major decision?

A. A decision reserved for approval by all partners or a defined majority, such as a budget change, a sale, new debt or a related-party contract, rather than left to the manager.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you are not running an energy trading company. But the mechanism that broke Enron is the same one that breaks small real estate partnerships: a person with a duty to the entity also profiting from deals with it, approved by people who did not look hard enough. The scale is different. The shape is identical. Cole joins me today because the warning signs were in the documents, for anyone who read them as an auditor would.

1. Timeline

Through the late 1990s Enron grew from a pipeline company into a trading business. In 1999 its chief financial officer, Andrew Fastow, set up private partnerships known as LJM, which he managed and invested in, and which then did deals with Enron. Enron's board approved this arrangement and waived the company's conflict-of-interest code to allow it. In August 2001 the chief executive, Jeffrey Skilling, resigned, and an internal employee, Sherron Watkins, wrote to the chairman, Kenneth Lay, warning that the accounting could implode. In October 2001 Enron reported a large third-quarter loss and a reduction in shareholder equity tied to the partnerships. In November it restated several years of earnings. On 2 December 2001 it filed for bankruptcy protection. Its auditor, Arthur Andersen, was later convicted over document destruction; that conviction was overturned on appeal in 2005, but the firm had already collapsed.

2. Key decisions

The decisive choice was the board's waiver. A conflict-of-interest code exists precisely to stop an officer from dealing with the company on his own account. Waiving it turned an exception into a structure. The second decision was to let the partnerships act as counterparties to hedges and asset sales that helped Enron's reported results. The third was relying on controls, such as reviews by other officers, without testing whether those controls actually operated.

3. Assumptions

The board assumed the review procedures it set would be followed. It assumed the partnerships were genuinely independent counterparties carrying real risk. Many investors assumed that a large audited company could not be hiding the substance of its results inside related entities. Each assumption was about a process, not about evidence that the process was working.

4. Incentives

The finance chief earned money from the partnerships, so he was paid on the other side of the table from his employer. Management was rewarded for reported earnings and a rising share price, which the deals supported. The auditor also earned substantial consulting fees from the client, which created pressure not to lose the relationship. When everyone's pay depends on the numbers looking good, no one is paid to say they are not.

5. Warning signs ignored

The waiver itself was the loudest sign. Others followed: earnings that grew while cash flow did not keep pace, financial disclosures about related parties that were very hard to read, and an employee's written warning to the chairman. Cole's point is simple. When a disclosure cannot be understood by a careful reader, that is not sophistication. That is a finding.

Say that out loud now.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was not the bankruptcy filing. It came when the reported results depended on the partnerships so heavily that unwinding them would reveal the losses. From then on, every quarter required more of the same structure to hold the picture together. Once the market lost trust in the numbers, credit and trading counterparties pulled back, and a trading business without counterparties cannot operate.

7. Root cause

The root cause was a governance failure: a person with a duty to the company was allowed to profit from transactions with it, and the people meant to supervise approved the structure and then relied on reports produced by those inside it. Accounting technique was the method. The permission was the cause.

Cole's view: reading it as an auditor

Here is how a small developer meets the same shape. This is a composite example. A managing partner of a hypothetical apartment joint venture owns a company that lends short-term bridge money to the project at a high rate, approved by the managing partner, reported in the managing partner's quarterly summary. The investors see "bridge finance cost" as one line. An auditor asks three questions: who is the lender, who approved the rate, and what would an independent lender have charged? If any answer is the managing partner, the control has failed, however honest the person is.

The second composite is quieter and more common. A sponsor's affiliated property manager charges the project a management fee above market and also books the leasing commissions. Each invoice is small and approved by the sponsor. Over five years the leakage is real money and it never appears as a single line anyone can argue about. The test is identical: who is paid, who approved it, and what would the market charge? Write the answers down and attach them to the quarterly report.

What a developer copies from this case

Three habits. First, a related-party register: a single list of every connected person and every contract with them, reviewed every quarter. Second, the market benchmark: for each item, a written note of what an independent party would charge, from a quote, a consultant or a published survey. Third, separation of approval: the person with the interest leaves the room, physically or on the call, while the others decide, and the minute says so. None of these needs a large firm. A spreadsheet, a quote and one line in the minutes are enough to prove the deal was clean, and to protect the honest partner from a later accusation.

There is a fourth habit, and it is the hardest. When someone inside your team raises a concern in writing, as an employee did at Enron, answer it formally, in writing, within a fixed time, and record what you checked. A warning that is acknowledged and investigated is a control working. A warning that is waved away becomes, later, the document that proves everyone knew.

The prevention rule

Rule 75: Never let anyone sit on both sides of a transaction with an entity they owe a duty to unless the relationship is disclosed in writing, the price is benchmarked independently, and a party with no interest approves it first.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is approving a conflict once because the person is trusted, and then never revisiting it. The control is a related-party register reviewed every quarter by the non-conflicted partners, with each item re-tested against market.

The beginner's mistake

Treating Enron as a story about clever accounting. Accounting was the method. The cause was permission given by a board to a conflicted officer.

Callback

In Week 71 we covered misrepresentation and fiduciary duty in investor reporting. Enron is the extreme case of both: reports that were technically drafted and substantively misleading, prepared by people with a stake in the outcome. The fiduciary standard asks what the reader needed to know, not what the drafter could defend.

Recap

Enron's board waived its conflict code, let its finance chief run partnerships that dealt with the company, and relied on reports from inside the structure. When trust in the numbers went, the business went with it. Rule 75 requires disclosure, an independent benchmark and non-conflicted approval for any deal across a duty.

Next: JAX, Deals, partners and investors, on The Money: what related-party dealing does to returns.
checklist: I keep a written related-party register for every project.
No one approves a deal in which they hold an interest.
Every related-party price has an independent benchmark on file.
I treat any disclosure I cannot understand as a finding, not as sophistication.
I compare reported profit with cash flow every quarter.
I give a written warning from inside the team a formal response within one week.
I check whether controls actually operated, not just whether they exist.
I never waive a conflict rule; I disclose and approve instead.
head: Field checklist
rule: Rule 75: Never let anyone sit on both sides of a transaction with an entity they owe a duty to unless the relationship is disclosed in writing, the price is benchmarked independently, and a party with no interest approves it first.
speak: Enron filed for bankruptcy in December 2001. Its board had allowed the chief financial officer to run outside partnerships that did deals with Enron itself, waiving the company's own conflict-of-interest code to do it. Those deals helped the reported results. The people supervising relied on reviews and reports produced from inside the structure. Warning signs were there: the waiver, earnings that ran ahead of cash, disclosures that careful readers could not understand, and an employee's written warning to the chairman. Once the results depended on the partnerships, unwinding them meant revealing losses, and when the market lost trust, counterparties left. The root cause was permission, not accounting. For a developer, the same shape appears when a managing partner lends to, builds for or manages the project through his own company. Rule 75: no one sits on both sides of a deal across a duty unless it is disclosed in writing, independently benchmarked and approved by someone with no interest.
terms: Waiver — a decision to set aside a rule for a particular case, which in governance should be rare, recorded and justified.
Counterparty — the other party to a transaction, whose independence matters when the deal is used to report results.
Restatement — a correction of previously published financial statements because they were materially wrong.

hostile.q: Your managing partner's company is lending to this project. How is that different from what went wrong at Enron?
hostile.a: The difference has to be in the controls, not in anyone's character. The loan is disclosed in writing to every investor, the rate was benchmarked against two independent lenders, and it was approved by the partners with no interest in the lender. It is on the related-party register reviewed every quarter, and any change to its terms needs the same approval again. If any of those were missing, your concern would be right.

title: What Related-Party Dealing Does to Returns
summary: A related-party markup is not a cost shared by everyone. It is a transfer from all the partners to one. This lesson measures that transfer in profit, equity multiple and value, and shows why the connected partner can come out ahead even while the project does worse.
body:
An above-market price paid to a connected party is not a project cost borne equally. It is a transfer of profit from every partner to one, and the numbers show why the connected partner can win while the project loses.

Recall

Q. What is the root cause of the Enron collapse, in one sentence?

A. A board allowed its finance chief to profit from deals with the company and then relied on reports prepared from inside that structure.

Q. Why does a developer keep a written pipeline of deals?

A. So that every opportunity has a stage, an owner and a next step, and so that decisions to pursue or drop a deal are recorded rather than remembered.

Q. What does a capital call do to a partner who does not fund it?

A. Depending on the agreement, the partner may be diluted, lose voting rights, or have the shortfall funded as a priority loan by the others. The mechanism must be written in advance.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, investors do not ask about related-party deals because they are suspicious of you. They ask because they have done this arithmetic before. Once you can do it too, you can explain your own affiliated arrangements with numbers, and you can spot the leak in anyone else's deal before you put money in.

Worked example one: the affiliated contractor

All figures hypothetical. A project costs 30,000,000 dollars in total and is worth 36,000,000 dollars on completion. Equity is 10,000,000 dollars: an investor puts in 9,000,000 and the sponsor puts in 1,000,000. Debt covers the remaining 20,000,000. For simplicity, profit is split in proportion to equity, 90 to 10, with no promote.

Step 1. Profit at market prices: 36,000,000 minus 30,000,000 equals 6,000,000 dollars. The equity multiple, which is total cash returned divided by cash invested, is 16,000,000 divided by 10,000,000, which is 1.6 times.

Step 2. Now the sponsor's own construction company wins the 20,000,000 dollar hard-cost contract at 1,000,000 dollars above a market bid. Total cost rises to 31,000,000. Profit falls to 5,000,000. The equity multiple falls to 15,000,000 divided by 10,000,000, which is 1.5 times.

Step 3. Who lost? The investor's share of profit falls from 5,400,000 to 4,500,000, a loss of 900,000 dollars. The sponsor's equity share falls from 600,000 to 500,000, a loss of 100,000 dollars.

Step 4. Who gained? The sponsor's company received the extra 1,000,000 dollars. So the sponsor, counting both pockets, is up 1,000,000 minus 100,000, which is 900,000 dollars. The investor is down exactly the same 900,000 dollars.

Say that out loud now.

That is the whole incentive problem in four lines. The smaller the sponsor's equity stake, the more a related-party markup pays the sponsor and the more it costs everyone else. A sponsor with 10 percent of the equity keeps 90 cents of every dollar of markup. This is why investors insist on independent benchmarks, and why a promote that rewards profit is a healthier way to pay a sponsor than a margin hidden in a contract.

Worked example two: the affiliated property manager

Leakage after completion is quieter, because it hits net operating income (NOI), the income left after operating costs and before debt and tax, and then gets multiplied by the market's capitalisation rate.

Step 1. The building earns 3,000,000 dollars a year in effective gross revenue. A market management fee is 3 percent, or 90,000 dollars. The sponsor's affiliated manager charges 4 percent, or 120,000 dollars. The difference is 30,000 dollars a year.

Step 2. NOI falls by 30,000 dollars a year.

Step 3. At a hypothetical cap rate of 6 percent, value equals NOI divided by the cap rate. 30,000 divided by 0.06 equals 500,000 dollars of lost value at sale.

So a one-point difference in a fee that nobody argued about costs the owners half a million dollars at exit, plus the 30,000 dollars a year in cash along the way. The fee percentages and the cap rate are commercial practice and vary by market and asset; the arithmetic does not.

Why the honest sponsor still documents everything

Suppose your affiliated contractor really is cheaper than the market. The arithmetic now runs in reverse and helps everyone. But you only get credit for it if you can prove it. An independent benchmark turns "trust me" into "here is the comparison". Lenders and investors will often accept an affiliated contractor on that basis, sometimes on condition that its margin and overhead are capped at agreed percentages and audited at completion. Those caps are commercial terms, negotiated deal by deal, not a standard.

Handshake deals have a money cost too. Every undocumented term is an option held by whichever partner benefits from reinterpreting it once values move. You cannot price that option precisely, but you can see its size: it is the gap between the two partners' versions, applied to the profit at risk. On Day 5 we will measure one.

What a sophisticated investor will ask for

Expect four requests, and offer them before you are asked. First, a list of every affiliated party and every contract with it, with values. Second, an independent benchmark for each. Third, a margin cap on affiliated construction, often expressed as a fee on cost plus reimbursement of actual, audited costs. Fourth, a right for the investor to replace the affiliate if it underperforms or if the sponsor is removed. Each of these is commercial practice, and the exact terms are negotiated.

A quick test you can run on any deal: divide the sponsor's total related-party income by the sponsor's equity cheque. In example one, the sponsor's affiliate earned an extra 1,000,000 dollars on a 1,000,000 dollar equity stake. A ratio near or above one means the sponsor can earn back its whole investment from the side contracts before the project makes a profit. That does not prove misconduct. It tells you where to look first.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

On your personal balance sheet, a related-party stream is concentration disguised as diversification. If your construction company, your management company and your equity in the project all depend on one building, you do not have three assets. You have one asset with three invoices. When the project struggles, all three fall together, and a dispute with your investors can reach all three at once. Record affiliated income separately from project equity, and ask what happens to each if the partnership ends badly. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any structuring decision.

Decision journals: a monthly thread

This month's thread is the decision journal from Week 2, applied to partners. Before you approve any related-party deal, write three lines: what you are deciding, the independent number you compared it with, and what would make you reverse the decision. Date it. In five years, that page is worth more than any memory.

It also protects you from yourself. When a deal is yours on both sides, your own judgment is the least reliable instrument in the room. The journal forces you to write the market number down before you see whether the answer suits you.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that related-party leakage is spread across many small lines, so no single number looks worth a fight. The control is to total every connected payment, each quarter, against its market benchmark, and report the sum.

The beginner's mistake

Looking only at the project's return and missing the transfer. A deal can show a decent IRR, the internal rate of return, while quietly moving a large share of the profit to one party.

Callback

In Week 38 we built waterfalls with preferred returns and promotes. A promote rewards the sponsor in the open, after investors are paid their hurdle. A related-party markup rewards the sponsor before anyone is paid, out of sight. Investors prefer the first for good reason.

Recap

A related-party markup transfers profit from all partners to the connected one, and the smaller the connected partner's stake, the larger the transfer. Fee leakage hits NOI and is multiplied by the cap rate at exit. Honest sponsors benchmark anyway, so they get credit when they are cheaper.

Next: Omar, Structure and governance, on The Rules: the law of conflicts, related-party approval and unwritten agreements.
checklist: I can show who gains and who loses from any related-party markup.
I total every connected payment against its market benchmark each quarter.
I convert any fee leakage into lost value using the cap rate.
I prefer an open promote to a hidden contract margin as sponsor pay.
I agree caps on affiliated margin and overhead where an affiliate is used.
I record affiliated income separately from my project equity.
I write a decision journal entry before approving any related-party deal.
I price the gap between two partners' versions of any unwritten term.
head: Field checklist
speak: A related-party markup is not a shared cost. It is a transfer. Take a hypothetical project with 10,000,000 dollars of equity, 90 percent from an investor and 10 percent from the sponsor. If the sponsor's own construction company charges 1,000,000 dollars above market, profit falls by 1,000,000. The investor loses 900,000 of profit share. The sponsor loses 100,000 of profit share but collects the full 1,000,000 through the contractor, so the sponsor is up 900,000. The smaller the sponsor's stake, the bigger that transfer. After completion the leak moves to fees: a property management fee one point above market on 3,000,000 dollars of revenue costs 30,000 a year, and at a 6 percent cap rate that is 500,000 dollars of value at sale. Honest sponsors document anyway, because an independent benchmark is the only way to get credit for being cheaper.
terms: Equity multiple — total cash returned to equity divided by total equity invested.
Capitalisation rate — the ratio of net operating income to value that the market uses to price a stabilised building.
Margin cap — an agreed limit on the profit and overhead an affiliated contractor or manager may charge, usually audited at completion.

hostile.q: Your affiliate takes a 4 percent management fee when the market is 3. Why should my capital pay for that?
hostile.a: It should not, unless the fee buys something the market rate does not. Here is the benchmark from two independent managers. If we cannot show the extra point buys better occupancy or lower costs, I will cut the fee to market or rebate the difference. And I have shown you what the extra point costs at exit, because at our cap rate it is roughly half a million dollars of value, not a rounding error.

title: Conflicts, Related-Party Approval and the Unwritten Agreement
summary: The law does not ban a partner from dealing with the partnership, but it does impose duties of loyalty and disclosure, and it treats some unwritten agreements as hard or impossible to enforce. This lesson explains the concepts, the clauses that make them work in a joint venture, and how two legal systems approach the point.
body:
The law rarely forbids a related-party deal outright. What it does is attach duties of loyalty and disclosure to the person on both sides, and make some unwritten agreements fragile, so your protection comes from following those duties and writing the terms into the agreement.

Recall

Q. In the affiliated-contractor example, why does a sponsor with a small equity stake gain from a markup?

A. Because the sponsor collects the whole markup through the affiliate but bears only its small equity share of the lost profit. The rest of the cost falls on the other partners.

Q. What is a finder's fee, and why must it be written down?

A. A fee paid to someone who introduces a deal. Without a written agreement, both the amount and whether it was earned become arguments after closing, and some jurisdictions restrict who may be paid for introducing certain deals.

Q. What is a deadlock clause for?

A. It sets out what happens when partners with equal votes cannot agree on a major decision, such as escalation to senior people, mediation, or a buy-sell mechanism, so the project does not freeze.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Days 1 to 3 showed the mechanisms and the money. Today is the legal frame that sits around them. You will not draft these clauses yourself, but you must know what they do, what to ask your lawyer for, and which questions only a lawyer in the right jurisdiction can answer. Everything here is concept. Verify each point against the primary source and with counsel before you rely on it.

The duty of loyalty, in plain English

When someone manages property or money for others, the law in many common-law systems expects them to act in the others' interest and not their own. That expectation is called a fiduciary duty, a duty of loyalty owed by a person who holds power over another's interests. Directors usually owe it to the company. Partners in a general partnership often owe duties of good faith to each other. The managing member of a joint venture vehicle may owe duties defined partly by statute and partly by the agreement itself.

The core idea is the no-conflict principle: a person with a fiduciary duty should not put themselves where their own interest conflicts with that duty, unless the people they owe it to give informed consent. Notice the exit built into that sentence. A conflict is usually not fatal. Undisclosed, unconsented conflict is the problem. That is why disclosure and independent approval are not courtesies. In many systems they are how a conflicted deal becomes a valid one.

Applied example, hypothetical. The managing member of a project company also owns the company that will supply windows. Many corporate statutes require a director with an interest in a material contract to disclose the nature and extent of that interest and not vote on it. If he discloses, leaves the vote, and the other directors approve on fair terms, the contract may stand. If he does none of that, the company may be able to set the contract aside or recover his profit. The exact requirements differ by statute and by entity type, so verify them against the governing law before relying on them.

What the joint venture agreement should say

Statute gives a floor. Your agreement builds the house. A sound related-party clause usually covers five things.

  1. A definition of related party wide enough to catch affiliates, relatives, entities under common control and anyone acting for a partner.
  2. A duty to disclose any proposed related-party transaction before it is made, with its terms.
  3. Classification of every related-party transaction as a major decision, approved only by the non-conflicted partners.
  4. A pricing standard: terms no less favourable than an arm's-length deal, supported by an independent benchmark.
  5. A remedy: what happens if the clause is breached, such as repayment of excess, removal as manager, or loss of a promote.

Say that out loud now.

Some agreements also let partners waive or narrow default fiduciary duties. That is a powerful clause. Before you accept a narrowing as an investor, or offer one as a sponsor, take advice, because a narrow duty plus a weak related-party clause leaves very little protection. Professional sign-off required: corporate and partnership lawyer.

The unwritten agreement

Oral agreements can be binding in many systems. But land is often treated differently. Many common-law jurisdictions require a contract for the sale of an interest in land to be evidenced in writing and signed, a rule descended from the old English Statute of Frauds. Courts have developed exceptions, such as part performance or estoppel, which can protect someone who acted in reliance on a promise. Those exceptions are fact-heavy and uncertain, which means expensive. Verify the writing requirement and its exceptions for the specific jurisdiction against the primary source before you rely on it.

So a handshake about contributing land, or about how contributed land will be valued, is fragile twice over. It may not be enforceable as a land contract, and even if it is, a court must decide which memory is true. The practical rule is the one from Day 1: put the economic terms in a signed document before value moves.

Six questions to put to your lawyer

You do not need the answers memorised. You need to ask the right questions, in writing, before you sign. Here are six, for any joint venture with a connected party.

  1. What duties does the manager owe us by default under the governing law, and does this agreement narrow or expand them?
  2. What disclosure and voting procedure does the statute require for an interested party, and does our agreement meet or exceed it?
  3. If a related-party deal is made without approval, what remedies are available: setting it aside, recovering profit, removing the manager, or damages?
  4. Is any part of our arrangement about land oral or informal, and if so, is it enforceable as it stands?
  5. Which jurisdiction's law governs the agreement, and which courts or arbitrators decide disputes?
  6. Do the investors and the sponsor each need separate counsel on this agreement?

The last question matters more than it looks. When one lawyer drafts for both sides of a related-party arrangement, the document can end up serving the drafter's client. Separate advice costs money up front and saves far more when a dispute arrives.

Two Systems

A conceptual comparison, to be verified against primary sources before reliance. Canada's common-law provinces and its federal corporate statute place duties of loyalty and care on directors and require disclosure of interests in material contracts, with Quebec applying its civil code alongside corporate statutes. Guyana is a common-law jurisdiction with some historical Roman-Dutch influence in property law, and its companies legislation is generally understood to follow a model similar to Canada's federal statute, including director conflict-disclosure provisions. Both systems use courts to enforce fiduciary duties and both recognise partnership duties. The practical differences that matter to you are in the detail: registration and filing requirements, how land transactions must be documented and registered, and how quickly and predictably courts resolve disputes. Verify against primary source, and take advice from counsel admitted in each jurisdiction.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming that because a conflicted deal is legal if disclosed, informal disclosure in a conversation is enough. The control is written disclosure, a recorded vote by non-conflicted parties, and a benchmark on file.

The beginner's mistake

Believing that a strong personal relationship replaces the related-party clause. The clause protects the relationship. Without it, the first disagreement about money becomes a disagreement about character.

Callback

In Week 20 LEX taught what binds in a letter of intent: some terms are binding, most are not, and the document itself must say which. The same discipline applies to a handshake term sheet for a joint venture. Write it, sign it, and state clearly which parts bind now.

Recap

Fiduciary duties of loyalty sit on anyone managing others' interests, and the no-conflict principle is usually satisfied by disclosure and informed, independent consent. The joint venture agreement should define related parties, require disclosure, make related-party deals major decisions, set an arm's-length standard and name a remedy. Unwritten land agreements are fragile. Verify every point against the primary source.

Next: Nadia, Accounting and reporting, on The Numbers: putting a price on a handshake.
checklist: I know whether the people managing my project owe fiduciary duties and to whom.
Every conflict is disclosed in writing before the decision, not after.
The conflicted party does not vote, and the minute records that.
My agreements define related party widely enough to catch affiliates and relatives.
Every related-party deal is a major decision with an arm's-length pricing standard.
The agreement names a remedy for breach of the related-party clause.
No land contribution or land valuation is left as an oral agreement.
I verify these points with counsel admitted in each jurisdiction.
head: Field checklist
speak: The law rarely bans a related-party deal. Instead, anyone managing other people's money or property often owes a fiduciary duty, a duty of loyalty. The no-conflict principle says they should not let their own interest clash with that duty unless the people they owe it to give informed consent. So disclosure and independent approval are not courtesies; they are often how a conflicted deal becomes valid. Statutes set a floor. The joint venture agreement should do more: define related parties widely, require written disclosure, make every related-party deal a major decision approved only by non-conflicted partners, require arm's-length terms backed by a benchmark, and name a remedy. Unwritten agreements are fragile, especially about land, which many common-law systems require to be evidenced in writing. Canada and Guyana both work from common-law foundations here, but the details differ. Verify every point against the primary source and with counsel.
terms: Fiduciary duty — a duty of loyalty owed by a person who holds power over another's money, property or interests.
No-conflict principle — the rule that a fiduciary should not place personal interest in conflict with the duty owed, without informed consent.
Arm's length — terms that independent parties, each acting in their own interest, would agree.

hostile.q: Your agreement narrows the manager's fiduciary duties. Why would any investor accept that?
hostile.a: Only if the related-party clause does the work the narrowed duty no longer does. In our draft every connected transaction is disclosed in writing, classified as a major decision, approved only by the investors, priced against an independent benchmark, and backed by a remedy that includes removal and loss of the promote. If you would prefer the default duties restored, I would rather discuss that now than defend a gap later. Both sides should take independent legal advice on this clause.

title: Putting a Price on a Handshake
summary: When two partners remember a land contribution differently, the gap can be measured in dollars of profit share. This lesson works through the distribution under each version, then prices the cost of fighting about it, and shows why one signed page is the cheapest asset in the deal.
body:
An unwritten term has a price. You can measure it as the gap between two partners' versions applied to the distribution, and you can measure the cost of fighting over it, and both numbers are usually larger than people expect.

Recall

Q. What is the no-conflict principle?

A. A person who owes a duty of loyalty should not put their own interest in conflict with that duty unless the people they owe it to give informed consent, which is why disclosure and independent approval matter.

Q. In business development, what is the difference between a lead and an opportunity?

A. A lead is a possible deal you have heard about. An opportunity is one you have qualified against your criteria and decided to pursue, with a named next step.

Q. What is a reporting covenant in a joint venture?

A. A promise by the manager to deliver defined reports, such as quarterly financials and budget variances, on a fixed timetable to the other partners.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, partners rarely fight about principles. They fight about a number that changed. If you can show both partners, early and in writing, what each version of an unwritten term is worth, you either settle it calmly or you discover that you should not be partners. Both outcomes are better than discovering it at sale.

Nadia's habit from twenty years of reconciling partner accounts is simple. Whenever a term can be read two ways, she does not argue about which reading is right. She computes both, puts them side by side on one page, and hands the page to the partners. Arguments about wording go on for months. A table with two columns usually ends the argument in one meeting, because each partner can see exactly what the other is asking for.

The setup

All figures hypothetical. Partner A contributes a site that cost 2,000,000 dollars. Partner B contributes 2,000,000 dollars of cash for design, permits and early costs. They agree by handshake to "value the land fairly". Two years later the site is rezoned and an appraiser values it at 3,500,000 dollars. The project is built with debt, completed and sold. After repaying all debt and costs, 9,000,000 dollars is left to distribute to the two partners.

Assume the distribution order, called the waterfall, is simple: first each partner gets its capital back, then remaining profit is split in proportion to capital. That order is an assumption for this example; real agreements vary and must be read.

Version 1: the land went in at cost

Step 1. Capital accounts. A holds 2,000,000 dollars, B holds 2,000,000 dollars. Total 4,000,000.

Step 2. Return of capital. Pay A 2,000,000 and B 2,000,000. Remaining: 9,000,000 minus 4,000,000 equals 5,000,000 dollars of profit.

Step 3. Split profit by capital, which is 50 to 50. Each receives 2,500,000.

Step 4. Totals. A receives 4,500,000. B receives 4,500,000. B's equity multiple is 4,500,000 divided by 2,000,000, which is 2.25 times.

Version 2: the land went in at its rezoned value

Step 1. Capital accounts. A holds 3,500,000, B holds 2,000,000. Total 5,500,000.

Step 2. Return of capital. Pay A 3,500,000 and B 2,000,000. Remaining: 9,000,000 minus 5,500,000 equals 3,500,000 dollars of profit.

Step 3. Split profit by capital. A's share is 3,500,000 divided by 5,500,000, about 63.6 percent. B's share is about 36.4 percent. A receives about 2,227,000 and B about 1,273,000.

Step 4. Totals. A receives about 5,727,000. B receives about 3,273,000. B's multiple falls to about 1.64 times.

Say that out loud now.

The price of the handshake is the difference: about 1,227,000 dollars moves from B to A, or back, depending only on which memory wins. Neither partner did anything different on site. One sentence, never written, decided more than a tenth of the money.

Version 3: the compromise nobody wrote down either

Partners often say "we are equal partners" in the same breath as "the land is valued fairly". Suppose the land went in at 3,500,000 but profit was split 50 to 50 because they were "equal". Return capital: A 3,500,000, B 2,000,000. Profit of 3,500,000 split equally: 1,750,000 each. A receives 5,250,000 and B 3,750,000. Now there are three defensible answers, each a few hundred thousand dollars from the next. That is what an unwritten term really is: not one disagreement, but a family of them.

The cost of fighting

Now price the dispute itself. All figures and probabilities hypothetical, for illustration only.

Step 1. B believes Version 1 is right. If B wins, B gains about 1,227,000 dollars over Version 2.

Step 2. B's lawyer thinks the chance of winning is roughly even, because the evidence is two memories. Expected gain: 1,227,000 times 0.5 equals about 614,000 dollars.

Step 3. B's legal costs through a contested hearing: say 300,000 dollars.

Step 4. The dispute freezes the sale for twelve months. The project carries 15,000,000 dollars of debt at 7 percent, so the extra interest is 1,050,000 dollars, which in this structure comes out of the distributable proceeds and so is borne half by each partner: 525,000 dollars for B.

Step 5. B's expected result from fighting: 614,000 minus 300,000 minus 525,000 equals about negative 211,000 dollars. A's position is the mirror image and also negative. Both lose by fighting, and the project's lender, broker and buyer all watch it happen.

The cheapest asset in the deal

Compare that with the cost of a one-page signed term sheet at the start, plus a few hours of a lawyer's time to confirm it: a small fraction of any of the numbers above. A written contribution value, a written profit split and a written waterfall would have produced one answer, Version 1, 2 or 3, chosen calmly when no value had moved.

When you review any partnership you are about to join, run this test. List every economic term. For each, ask: is it written, signed and unambiguous? For each one that is not, write the two plausible versions and compute the distribution under both. The gap is your exposure. If it is large, fix the document before you fund.

A second worked example: the related-party fee test

The same method works on a written but unbenchmarked term. All figures hypothetical. A sponsor's affiliate charges a development management fee of 4 percent of hard and soft costs on a 25,000,000 dollar project. An independent survey of comparable projects suggests 3 percent.

Step 1. Fee charged: 25,000,000 times 0.04 equals 1,000,000 dollars.

Step 2. Benchmark fee: 25,000,000 times 0.03 equals 750,000 dollars.

Step 3. Excess: 250,000 dollars, paid before any partner sees a profit.

Step 4. If the sponsor holds 10 percent of the equity, the sponsor bears 25,000 of the excess as lost profit and keeps 250,000 through the affiliate. Net transfer to the sponsor: 225,000 dollars.

The fee percentages here are commercial practice, not a standard, and vary with project size and scope. What matters is the method: charged, benchmark, excess, and who carries it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that no one computes the gap until the value has already moved, when each partner is anchored to the version that pays them more. The control is to run the two-version calculation at signing and attach it to the term sheet.

The beginner's mistake

Assuming the waterfall is obvious. Return of capital first, profit by capital, profit equally, a preferred return: each gives a different answer. Write which one applies.

Callback

In Week 33 JAX and Omar taught how to value contributed land in a landowner joint venture: at cost, at appraisal, or at an agreed figure with an adjustment mechanism. Today shows why that choice must be made, and written, before rezoning, not after.

Recap

A handshake on land value moved about 1,227,000 dollars in this hypothetical, and a compromise version created a third answer. Fighting about it cost both partners more than they could expect to win. One signed page at the start is the cheapest asset in the deal.

Next: Cole, Audit and integrity, on The Room: the meeting where a partner proposes a related-party contract.
checklist: I list every economic term in a partnership before I fund it.
For each unwritten term I write the two plausible versions.
I compute the distribution under each version and record the gap.
I confirm the waterfall order in writing, step by step.
I fix the contribution value of land before any rezoning or approval.
I price the cost of a dispute, including delay interest, before choosing to fight.
I attach the two-version calculation to the signed term sheet.
I take legal advice to confirm which terms bind.
head: Field checklist
speak: An unwritten term has a price. Take a hypothetical joint venture. Partner A contributes land that cost 2,000,000 dollars, Partner B contributes 2,000,000 in cash, and they agree by handshake to value the land fairly. The site is rezoned and appraised at 3,500,000. After sale, 9,000,000 dollars is left to distribute. Return capital first, then split profit by capital. With land at cost, each partner gets 4,500,000. With land at the rezoned value, A gets about 5,727,000 and B about 3,273,000. One unwritten sentence moves about 1,227,000 dollars. Now price the fight. If B has an even chance of winning, the expected gain is about 614,000. Subtract 300,000 of legal costs and 525,000 of B's share of a year's extra interest, and B expects to lose about 211,000. Both partners lose by fighting. A signed page at the start would have cost almost nothing.
terms: Capital account — the running record of what each partner has contributed and is owed back before profit is shared.
Waterfall — the agreed order in which distributable cash is paid out to partners.
Expected value — the probability-weighted average outcome of an uncertain choice.

hostile.q: You want to value your land at the rezoned figure. Why should my cash take a smaller share of the profit?
hostile.a: Here are both versions, computed in full. At cost, we split evenly; at the appraised value, the profit share moves about 1.2 million dollars toward me. I would rather we choose one now, in writing, than argue at sale. My proposal is the appraised value with a lower profit split for the land, so your cash earns a preferred return first. If that does not work for you, tell me which version does, and we will document it before any more money moves.

title: The Meeting Where a Partner Proposes His Own Company
summary: A co-developer proposes that his own company take a large contract on the joint project. This lesson scripts the meeting: what to say, what never to say, the question behind his question, when to be silent, and how to hold your state so the conversation stays about controls, not character.
body:
When a partner proposes his own company for a project contract, your job in the room is to turn a question about trust into a question about process, calmly, without accusing him and without agreeing to anything that has not been benchmarked.

Recall

Q. In the handshake example, how much did one unwritten sentence move between the partners?

A. About 1,227,000 dollars in that hypothetical, depending only on whether the land went in at cost or at its rezoned value.

Q. What is the first thing to establish with a new landowner contact?

A. What they actually want from the land, which may be income, a lump sum, legacy or staying involved, because that shapes the whole structure of the offer.

Q. What is a tag-along right?

A. A right for a minority partner to sell on the same terms when a majority partner sells, so they are not left behind with a new partner they did not choose.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will be in this room more than once, and sometimes you will be the one proposing your own affiliate. The skill is identical from both chairs. A related-party proposal handled well builds trust; handled badly, it starts the slow slide toward governance capture we saw on Day 1. The words in the first ten minutes decide which way it goes.

The scene

This is a composite example. You and a co-developer each hold half of a hypothetical joint venture building a small residential project. The design is nearly done. At the monthly partners' meeting, he says: "My framing company can do the structure for 3,000,000 dollars. We know the drawings, we can start in two weeks, and frankly it keeps the money in the family. I'd like to sign it this week so we hold the schedule." Your agreement makes related-party contracts a major decision. He knows that. He is asking you to approve it in this meeting.

The question behind the question

On the surface he is asking for approval. Underneath he may be asking several things at once. Do you trust me? Will you slow the schedule? Will you let me earn a contractor's margin as well as my share of the profit? Sometimes the honest answer to the hidden question is yes, his company really is the best option. The process exists so that you can say yes to the right answer without anyone, including a future lender or buyer, wondering why.

The lines to say

Open with the thing you agree on. "I want the schedule held as much as you do, and your team knowing the drawings is a real advantage."

Then move to process, not character. "Because it's your company, our agreement treats it as a major decision. Let's do it properly so nobody can question it later, including the lender."

Name the three steps. "I'd like a written disclosure of your interest, an independent benchmark, either two outside bids or our cost consultant's estimate, and then I'll decide as the non-conflicted partner."

Offer a date. "If we ask for two bids today, we can decide in ten working days. Can the start slip a week if we need it?"

Say that out loud now.

If the benchmark comes back close to his price, say so plainly and approve it on terms: "Your number is within range. I'll approve it with an open-book margin cap and the contract on the related-party register."

If he asks, "So you think I'd overcharge?", answer the process, not the accusation: "No. I think a lender, a buyer and our own future selves will ask how we chose, and I want the answer on paper." That reply keeps both of you on the same side of the table.

The lines never to say

Never say "I don't trust you" or "this looks like a conflict". The first insults him; the second states a conclusion. Never say "just this once" or "fine, we're friends". Both create the precedent that the next related-party deal will cite. Never negotiate his price in the meeting without a benchmark, because any number you agree becomes the anchor, a figure that pulls the rest of the discussion toward it. And never agree verbally and promise to do the paperwork later. The paperwork is the approval.

When to stay silent

After you have named the three steps, stop. He may push back: "It'll cost us two weeks." Let the silence sit for a few seconds before answering. Silence tells him the process is not a bargaining position. When you do answer, answer the schedule point only: "Two weeks of bids is cheaper than a year of questions from the lender." Then stop again.

Stay silent too when he offers a concession you did not ask for, such as "I'll knock 5 percent off". Thank him, and say the benchmark will tell you both whether 5 percent is the right number. A price that drops before anyone has tested it is information, not a reason to approve.

Holding your state

You may feel two pulls: the wish to keep the friendship smooth, and irritation at being rushed. Both push you toward a quick answer. Before the meeting, decide your position in writing: no related-party contract without disclosure, benchmark and recorded approval. In the room, slow your speech and keep your voice level. If you notice heat rising, ask a factual question, such as "What's the margin built into the 3,000,000?" Questions return you to analysis. Afterwards, write the minute that day, while both of you remember the same meeting.

A worked example of the follow-up

Ten days later, all figures hypothetical. Two outside bids arrive at 3,150,000 and 3,250,000 dollars. The cost consultant estimates 3,100,000. His 3,000,000 is below all three. The answer is yes. You approve it with three conditions: an open-book margin cap of 8 percent on cost, which is a negotiated term and not a standard; change orders above 50,000 dollars need your approval; and the contract goes on the register with the benchmark attached. You now have a better price, a documented decision and a stronger partnership. The process did not slow the good deal. It proved it.

How the best do it

Well-run institutional partnerships keep a standing related-party protocol, so nobody has to invent the process in a tense meeting. The protocol names who benchmarks, how many bids are needed, who votes and what goes in the minute. Because it is written in advance, invoking it is never personal. A small developer can copy that by attaching a one-page protocol to every joint venture agreement.

Working with advisers: a monthly thread

This is where your cost consultant earns their fee. Instruct them in writing, tell them who pays them and who they report to, and ask for their benchmark before either partner has seen the related-party price, so the number cannot be shaped to fit. An adviser who knows the answer you want is less useful than one who does not.

And when advice comes back that you dislike, ask for the reasoning, not a softer conclusion. The value of an independent adviser in this room is precisely that their job does not depend on either partner's approval.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is approving under schedule pressure in the meeting itself. The control is a pre-agreed protocol and a written position decided before you walk in.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the question as personal and either caving to avoid offence or refusing to avoid risk. The process lets you say yes to a good deal and no to a bad one without either being about character.

Callback

In Week 66 Kema and JAX taught interests versus positions. His position is "sign this week". His interests are schedule, margin and recognition. Today's script meets the interests, schedule through a short timetable and margin through a cap, without accepting the position.

Recap

Agree on the shared goal, move to process, name disclosure, benchmark and non-conflicted approval, then be silent. Never accuse, never anchor, never approve verbally. Write the minute the same day.

Next: Kema, Chief of staff and learning coach, on Quiz and Recap for the second post-mortem week.
checklist: I decide my related-party position in writing before the meeting.
I open with the goal we share, then move to process.
I ask for written disclosure, an independent benchmark and a recorded vote.
I never negotiate a related-party price without a benchmark in hand.
I never approve verbally and promise paperwork later.
I stay silent after stating the process.
I instruct the benchmark adviser before either side sees the proposed price.
I write the minute the same day.
head: Field checklist
speak: When a partner proposes his own company for a project contract, turn a question about trust into a question about process. Start with what you share: you both want the schedule held. Then say that, because it is his company, the agreement makes it a major decision, so you will do it properly. Name three steps: written disclosure of his interest, an independent benchmark such as two outside bids or the cost consultant's estimate, and a decision by you as the non-conflicted partner, with a date. Then stop talking. Never say you do not trust him, never call it a conflict, never agree just this once, and never negotiate the price before the benchmark arrives, because any number you say becomes the anchor. If the benchmark shows his price is good, approve it with a margin cap, change-order limits and a place on the related-party register. Write the minute the same day.
terms: Anchor — the first number put into a negotiation, which tends to pull later numbers toward it.
Open-book margin cap — an agreed maximum profit on the contractor's actual, auditable costs.
Related-party protocol — a pre-written procedure for disclosing, benchmarking and approving connected contracts.

hostile.q: Your partner's company built the structure. How do I know the joint venture didn't overpay?
hostile.a: Here is the file. His written disclosure, two independent bids at 3,150,000 and 3,250,000 dollars, our cost consultant's estimate of 3,100,000, his price of 3,000,000, and the minute recording that I approved it as the non-conflicted partner with an 8 percent open-book margin cap. Every change order over 50,000 dollars came to me, and they are all listed. You do not need to take my word for any of it.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Post-Mortem II: Six Questions on Partnership Failure
summary: Six questions test the week: the three internal failure mechanisms, Enron's root cause, the arithmetic of related-party dealing, the duty of loyalty, the price of a handshake and the meeting script. A Red Pen drill on a flawed joint venture clause and a two-minute boardroom drill close the week.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: partnerships fail from inside when control, conflicts or terms go unchecked, and the cure in every case is disclosure, an independent number and a signature, applied before value moves.

Recall

Q. In the Room lesson, what should you do right after naming the three-step process?

A. Stop talking. Let silence show that the process is not a bargaining position.

Q. What is a referral relationship in business development?

A. A standing relationship, often with a broker, lawyer or banker, that sends you deal flow, maintained by giving value back, not only by asking.

Q. What is a drag-along right?

A. A right for a majority partner to require minority partners to sell on the same terms when the majority sells the whole venture.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is the second of four post-mortem weeks. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer. If you hesitate, reread that day's lesson tomorrow.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the three ways a partnership fails from inside.

Answer: Governance capture, where control drifts into one partner's hands; related-party dealing, where one partner sits on both sides of a deal; and handshake deals, where key terms exist only in memory. Each feels like efficiency while it is happening.

Question 2. What was the root cause of the Enron collapse?

Answer: A governance failure. The board waived its conflict code, allowed the finance chief to profit from partnerships that dealt with the company, and relied on reports produced from inside that structure. The accounting was the method; the permission was the cause.

Question 3. Why does a sponsor with a small equity stake gain from a related-party markup?

Answer: The sponsor collects the whole markup through the affiliate but bears only its equity share of the lost profit. In the hypothetical, a 1,000,000 dollar markup cost the 10 percent sponsor 100,000 and paid it 1,000,000, a net gain of 900,000, equal to the investor's loss.

Question 4. What is the no-conflict principle, and how is a conflicted deal usually made valid?

Answer: A person owing a duty of loyalty should not put personal interest in conflict with that duty without informed consent. In many systems the deal is made valid by written disclosure, abstention from the vote, and approval on fair terms by those without an interest. Verify the exact requirements against the primary source.

Question 5. How do you price an unwritten term?

Answer: Write the two plausible versions, compute the distribution under each, and take the gap. Then price a dispute: probability-weighted gain, minus legal costs, minus your share of delay costs. In the example, fighting had a negative expected value for both partners.

Question 6. What do you say, and not say, when a partner proposes his own company?

Answer: Say what you share, then name the process: written disclosure, an independent benchmark, a decision by the non-conflicted partner, and a date. Never accuse, never say "just this once", never negotiate the price before the benchmark, and never approve verbally.

Recap of the week

Day 1 named the three mechanisms. Day 2 took Enron through seven steps and produced Rule 75. Day 3 measured the transfer a related-party markup creates. Day 4 set out fiduciary duty, related-party clauses and the fragility of oral land agreements, with Canada and Guyana compared. Day 5 priced a handshake and a dispute. Day 6 scripted the meeting.

Red Pen

Read this hypothetical joint venture clause and find the defects before reading on.

"The Manager may engage any Affiliate to provide services to the Venture provided the fees are reasonable. The Manager shall inform the Partners of any such engagement in the next annual report. For this purpose, Affiliate means any company in which the Manager holds a majority of the shares. The land contributed by Partner A shall be valued fairly."

Say that out loud now.

The defects. First, "reasonable" has no benchmark; it should require arm's-length terms supported by an independent quote or consultant. Second, the Manager engages the affiliate alone; the clause must make it a major decision approved by non-conflicted partners. Third, disclosure comes after the fact, in an annual report; it must come before the engagement, in writing. Fourth, the definition of Affiliate is too narrow: it misses minority stakes, relatives, common control and nominees. Fifth, there is no remedy for breach. Sixth, "valued fairly" is a handshake written down; it must state a number, or a method and a date, such as an appraisal as at signing.

A second pass: the minute that follows

Now read the minute a manager might write after approving an affiliate, and find what is missing.

"Partners discussed the framing contract. It was agreed that the Manager's company would proceed at the quoted price, which all felt was competitive. Paperwork to follow."

The defects. It does not name the Manager's interest or record that it was disclosed. It does not say who voted, or that the Manager abstained. "All felt was competitive" is an opinion, not a benchmark; the minute should name the independent bids or estimate and their figures. "Paperwork to follow" means the approval has not yet happened in any form a lender or buyer will accept. A good minute states the interest, the benchmark, the vote, the conditions such as a margin cap, and the date the signed contract was placed on the register.

The habit to take from both drills is to read every governance document asking one question: if a stranger read only this page in five years, could they tell who decided, on what evidence, and whether anyone in the decision had an interest? If the page cannot answer, the control did not operate, however good the intentions were.

The boardroom drill

Set a two-minute timer. Explain to an imagined investment committee how you control related-party risk in a joint venture. Then compare with this model answer.

"Our partnerships fail from inside, not from the market, in three ways: captured control, related-party deals and unwritten terms. We control each in writing. Major decisions are defined by substance, and partners see the bank and contract records directly. Every related-party deal is disclosed in advance, benchmarked against independent quotes, approved only by partners without an interest, priced at arm's length, and listed on a register we review each quarter. Affiliated contractors work under an open-book margin cap. Contributed land is valued by a stated method at signing, before any rezoning, and the waterfall is spelled out step by step. The reason is arithmetic: a sponsor with 10 percent of the equity keeps 90 cents of every dollar of markup, so investors are right to ask. We would rather show the file than ask for trust."

Score yourself. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you name all three mechanisms and a control for each? Did you give one number? Did you finish in two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is learning these controls and applying them to other people's deals but not your own. The control is to run the Red Pen on your own agreements first.

The beginner's mistake

Memorising Rule 75 without the three parts that make it work: disclosure, an independent benchmark and non-conflicted approval. Leave out one, and the rule is decoration.

Callback

In Week 46, the first post-mortem, the failures were about leverage and maturity walls. This week the money was often fine and the governance failed. Put the two weeks together and you have the two ways most developers lose a project: too much debt, or too little control.

Recap

Three mechanisms, one rule, one arithmetic of transfer, one legal frame, one priced handshake and one script. Disclose, benchmark, approve, and write it before value moves.

head: The six questions
speak: This week was about how partnerships fail from inside. Three mechanisms: governance capture, related-party dealing and handshake deals. Enron showed the extreme case, where a board waived its conflict code and let its finance chief profit from deals with the company. Rule 75 says no one sits on both sides of a deal across a duty unless it is disclosed in writing, independently benchmarked and approved by someone with no interest. The arithmetic explains why investors care: a sponsor with 10 percent of the equity keeps 90 cents of every dollar of markup. The law usually allows a conflicted deal if it is disclosed and approved by those without an interest, and it treats unwritten land deals as fragile. A handshake can be priced: compute both versions and take the gap. In the room, agree on the goal, name the process, then stay silent. Disclose, benchmark, approve, and write it down before value moves.
terms: Related-party register — a single list of every connected party and every contract with them, reviewed regularly by non-conflicted partners.
Red Pen — a drill in which you read a short document looking for planted defects before they are revealed.
Major decision — a decision reserved for approval by all partners or a defined majority rather than the manager alone.

hostile.q: You keep talking about controls. Have you ever approved a related-party deal that turned out badly?
hostile.a: The honest answer is that the controls exist because the risk is real for everyone, including me. What I can show you is the file for every related-party deal in our ventures: the disclosure, the benchmark and the approval by partners without an interest. If one of them had gone wrong, that file is what would let us see where, and it is what would let you hold me to account. I would rather be judged on the file than on my reassurance.
